name: Correctness
question: Does it do what it says it does?
look_for: Check each claim in the code, comments, commit message and docs against the code itself and against the sources it cites. Run it, or its tests, where that is safe. Look for wrong results, wrong conditions, off-by-one errors, unhandled errors and race conditions.
standard: The ticket or request it was written for, and the house rules (review.py rules)

name: Regressions
question: What worked before that this change could break?
look_for: Find the callers of anything changed or removed. Check public contracts: endpoints, database objects an API reads, file formats, command flags and defaults. Look for tests that were deleted, loosened or changed just to pass. Use the git history (log -S, blame, co-change) to find what used to depend on it. Run the tests on the base and on the change when you can.
standard: The project's public contracts and tests, and the house rules. For an API, its published spec or changelog. Walk the history in references/sources.md finds what used to depend on it

name: Completeness
question: Does it cover the whole ask?
look_for: Check every acceptance criterion in the ticket. Check error paths, and empty or unusual input. Look for tests of the new behaviour. Look for docs, database migrations and config that should have changed with it. Check every operating system and tool it claims to support.
standard: The ticket and its acceptance criteria, and the house rules for what a change must carry

name: Code quality
question: Would the team accept this as written?
look_for: Apply the team's standard for the language. Check readability, naming, duplication, robustness, performance and security. Skip what the analyzer or linter already enforces, and say which one ran.
standard: The house rules first, then the repo's own linter and style configs (review.py configs), then the language's public style guide, such as PEP 8 https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/ or the Google style guides https://google.github.io/styleguide/. For security, OWASP Top 10 https://owasp.org/Top10/ and OWASP ASVS https://owasp.org/www-project-application-security-verification-standard/

name: References and docs
question: Do the links, citations and docs hold up?
look_for: Every link, path and file reference resolves. Each cited source says what the text claims, so read the source. The docs match what the code does now. The examples actually run.

name: Dynamic or hardcoded
question: Will anything go stale, or only suit one kind of user?
look_for: Look for hardcoded versions, counts, URLs, names, model names, dates, paths and lists that change over time. Look for defaults that only fit one operating system, role, team or tool. Each one needs a lookup when it is used, or a checked date and a way to check it again.
standard: Wherever the value really lives: the tool's own docs, the system of record, or the machine

name: Perspectives
question: Who will meet this change, and what would each of them notice that the author did not?
look_for: First work out who and what this particular change will meet, from the diff, the ticket and the repository: who uses it, runs it, supports it, integrates with it, pays for it, audits it or maintains it, and where it runs (operating system, browser, device, locale and language, scale, accessibility needs, other AI tools). Pick the three to five that matter most for this change and say in one line why each one matters here. Add every perspective a house rule names. Then read the change as each of them. Report only what the other lenses missed. A new starter, a Windows user or the on-call engineer are examples, not a fixed list.
standard: The people who will actually use or maintain it, and any house rule about who reads it
